Oxygen-16 geometry: a visual and numerical audit¶

This notebook follows the current geometry engine from nucleon positions in three dimensions to hotspots, Gaussian densities, and longitudinally integrated thickness. It compares the tetrahedral alpha model with the spherical three-parameter Fermi model. “WS / 3pF” below means the repository's O16_3PF: its nonzero $w$ makes it a three-parameter Fermi profile, rather than a two-parameter Woods–Saxon profile.

Run all cells after changing the geometry code. Every physics sample and field evaluation calls upcmodel; notebook helpers handle plotting, numerical integration, and independent diagnostics. The fixed seed and exported samples make a suspicious event reproducible. Changing a view never resamples it.

Reading guide

  1. Parameters, units, and the input radial distribution.
  2. Tetrahedral construction and rotations; 3D events and 2D projections.
  3. Ensemble radii and shape fluctuations; pair distances.
  4. Hotspot parents, weights, multiplicity, widths, and $x$ dependence.
  5. Density slices and thickness maps; rotatable 3D explorers.
  6. Explicit $z$ integration; normalization; ensemble fields; audit results.

1. Reproducible setup¶

The defaults give thousands of inexpensive geometry events and a smaller set of more expensive field evaluations. Increase the ensemble sizes for statistics; increase map or volume resolution for spatial detail. The interactive HTML explorers use Plotly, while every main comparison also has a saved static figure.

Parameters and length scales¶

The alpha-center radius is the distance from the nuclear center to a tetrahedron vertex. The alpha nucleon width describes sampling nucleons around that vertex. The hotspot offset width describes sampling hotspots around a nucleon. The profile width describes smearing an already sampled source.

For this notebook the non-hotspot profile uses $\sigma_N^2=B_p+B_{\rm hs}$ in fm$^2$. Convolution of the Gaussian hotspot-center distribution with a hotspot Gaussian gives this width, so the smooth profile matches the conditional mean of the hotspot profile at fixed nucleon positions. This is an explicit comparison choice, editable in the setup cell. It does not change any engine parameter or enforce equality between individual fluctuating events.

Why the final radial distribution can differ from the input¶

The input 3pF function describes independent proposals. Rejecting an entire event with a close pair conditions this distribution; subtracting that event's center of mass changes its radii again. The control below shows each operation on the same proposal pool. Agreement of the raw sample with the input is a sampler check. Exact agreement of the final recentered ensemble with the input is not an expected invariant.

Control proposals accepted: 2846/4000 (71.2%); raw empirical CDF discrepancy 0.0021

3. Tetrahedron and rotations¶

The ideal vertices have radius $R_\alpha$ and common edge length $\sqrt{8/3}\,R_\alpha$. The actual four-nucleon cluster means fluctuate around the construction centers. The sampler returns nucleons, not its original construction centers; dashed tetrahedra on sampled events connect observed cluster means, which need not form a regular tetrahedron.

A uniform orientation requires uniform $\cos\theta$ and azimuth, not uniform $\theta$. The rotation checks also verify $R^\mathsf{T}R=I$ and $\det R=+1$.

Rotation diagnostic: mean direction [ 0.0022 -0.0099  0.0056] ; second moments [0.3375 0.3347 0.3278] (expected 0 and 1/3).

4. One event in 3D, viewed from three directions¶

Both rows use the same physical axis scale. Circles are protons, triangles are neutrons. Alpha colors identify the four parent clusters; WS colors distinguish protons and neutrons. Changing the camera preserves the sampled configuration. The black plus marks the nuclear center of mass.

All three Cartesian projections¶

These are projections of the same 3D centers onto XY, XZ, and YZ. In particular, two centers may overlap in XY while remaining far apart in 3D. The dashed alpha connections again join observed cluster means.

5. Ensemble radii, orientation, and shape fluctuations¶

All histograms in this section use nucleon centers. A Gaussian matter profile adds its own width: for unit weights, $\langle r^2\rangle_{\rho}=\langle r_{\rm center}^2\rangle+3\sigma_N^2$ and $\langle b^2\rangle_T=\langle b_{\rm center}^2\rangle+2\sigma_N^2$. Keep this difference in mind when comparing a plotted field radius with a histogram of center radii.

An isotropic ensemble should have matching $x,y,z$ distributions and uniform $z/r$. An individual event can be strongly anisotropic.

For the following geometric diagnostics, $\varepsilon_n=|\sum_j(x_j+i y_j)^n|/\sum_j b_j^n$ for $n=2,3$. These are recentered, unit-weight point-nucleon moments; they are not flow coefficients or dipole amplitudes. A charge-only center of mass can fluctuate away from the nuclear center because it uses only eight of the sixteen nucleons.

6. Hard-core and cluster-distance diagnostics¶

The exclusion distance applies to 3D nucleon pairs, including pairs in different alpha clusters. It creates no minimum allowed projected separation. The same-cluster and different-cluster curves below each integrate to one; their pair counts differ, so they should not be added without pair-count weights.

7. Attach hotspots to the sampled nucleons¶

For each event the engine returns hotspot centers $(M,3)$, parent IDs $(M,)$, weights $(M,)$, and positive multiplicities $(16,)$. The number of hotspots $M$ fluctuates. Every parent contributes total weight one, so the target weight remains $A=16$.

The three-dimensional offsets use $\sigma_{\rm offset}=\sqrt{B_p}$ after unit conversion. Each hotspot later receives the narrower Gaussian profile $\sigma_{\rm hs}=\sqrt{B_{\rm hs}}$. No extra recentering or hard-core exclusion is applied to hotspots.

Multiplicity and width diagnostics¶

The function mean_hotspot_count returns the underlying Poisson rate $\lambda(x)$. The conditional mean after rejecting zero is $\mu=\lambda/(1-e^{-\lambda})$. Its variance is $(\lambda+\lambda^2)/(1-e^{-\lambda})-\mu^2$. The offset distributions must instead have variance $B_p$ in each coordinate. The weighted hotspot center of mass is allowed to fluctuate around the nuclear center; forcing it to zero would alter the event fluctuations.

Energy parameter scan on fixed nucleon configurations¶

The scan changes the hotspot distribution through $\lambda(x)=p_0x^{p_1}(1+p_2\sqrt{x})$. Each displayed $x$ uses one independent hotspot realization around the same nucleons. Thus a single pixel or peak need not change monotonically with $x$. Every map still has total target weight 16. For the small-rate control, the difference between the underlying and zero-truncated distributions is especially visible.

The hotspot parameterization is documented in the engine and in the model reference, equations 10–14. The values displayed here always come from the repository's parameter objects.

8. Gaussian fields: density slices and integrated thickness¶

For a fixed set of centers $\mathbf r_k=(\mathbf b_k,z_k)$, $$ \rho(\mathbf r)=\sum_k\frac{w_k}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{3/2}} e^{-|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_k|^2/(2\sigma^2)},\qquad T(\mathbf b)=\sum_k\frac{w_k}{2\pi\sigma^2} e^{-|\mathbf b-\mathbf b_k|^2/(2\sigma^2)}. $$ Both full integrals equal $\sum_k w_k=A$. The transverse exponent and the two-dimensional normalization already include the analytic integration over $z$. Each source's $z_k$ therefore disappears from the thickness.

Each pair of model rows uses shared color scales for the same quantity and profile mode. Density and thickness have separate color scales because their units differ. The plotted window includes at least six smooth-profile widths outside the example source centers.

Main map extent ±6 fm; spacing 0.0667 fm; hotspot sigma 0.1765 fm.

Thickness as a surface¶

The vertical coordinate in these plots is thickness, in fm$^{-2}$; it is not the physical longitudinal coordinate $z$. Section 12's density-volume explorer uses physical $x,y,z$ coordinates.

Follow the density through several longitudinal slices¶

Moving a slice through $z$ selects different parts of a fixed event. In contrast, the thickness includes every slice. All panels in each profile-mode group share one density color scale.

Projection changes under a physical rotation¶

Here the configuration is rotated, while the beam direction stays along $z$. Nucleons and their already sampled hotspots rotate together. This can change the thickness because a different 3D column is projected. It differs from merely moving the 3D camera, and from rotating the whole image within the XY plane.

9. Integrate the actual 3D density over z¶

This numerical calculation evaluates position_to_gaussian_density on $(x,y,z)$ points and integrates its output with the trapezoid rule. It is independent of the analytic thickness evaluator. The $z$ interval extends eight profile widths beyond every source center; the grid is refined from roughly $2\sigma$ to $\sigma/2$.

The left panels show a longitudinal density column through the highest-thickness pixel of each example. The right panels compare analytic and numerical thickness along $y=0$. The area under a left-hand curve is a thickness, not a 3D density.

Separate longitudinal window loss from grid-spacing error¶

A coarse grid can miss a narrow Gaussian even when its integration window is large. A fine grid with too small a window instead loses genuine Gaussian tails. The window-loss curves below use exact Gaussian CDFs at the selected columns; the spacing curves use numerical integration of the engine's 3D density. Very small errors are shown at a plotting floor of $10^{-16}$.

10. Full normalization and transformation audit¶

The next cell integrates the engine's 3D density on a Cartesian volume, then compares it with a transverse integral of its thickness. Each volume extends seven profile widths beyond all centers, with spacing no larger than $\sigma/2$. An independent finite-box Gaussian-CDF result distinguishes quadrature error from the tiny amount of probability outside the box.

This is the most expensive validation cell. It evaluates points in chunks so a large points-by-sources-by-coordinates array is never allocated for the full volume.

Transverse resolution check¶

Coarse sampling can both overestimate and underestimate a narrow Gaussian, depending on the phase of the grid relative to its centers. The two grid origins below expose this aliasing. The fine-grid result should approach the independent finite-window integral for both choices. This is separate from the resolution of the illustrative 3D explorer.

11. Ensemble mean and fluctuations of the thickness¶

The maps below reuse the first field-ensemble events of each model. Smooth and hotspot profiles use exactly the same underlying nucleons. The right column shows the sample standard deviation of the hotspot thickness across events, not the standard error of its mean and not an incoherent cross section.

Finite samples need not give perfectly circular mean maps. The two models are rotationally invariant as ensembles even though their individual events are not.

Hotspot averaging at fixed nucleon positions¶

This control holds the nucleons fixed and averages independent hotspot realizations. Because every parent carries unit weight, the ensemble mean is the Gaussian convolution with variance $B_p+B_{\rm hs}$, irrespective of the sampled hotspot count. The finite-sample residual should shrink statistically as more independent configurations are added; it need not decrease at every step. This explains the smooth-width convention chosen at the top of the notebook.

12. Rotatable 3D explorers¶

The two standalone HTML files work without a running notebook kernel or an internet connection. Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, and hover for coordinates. Both model panels use matching physical axis scales. Use the standalone links for a full-size view, including in notebook frontends that restrict embedded local HTML.

The first explorer shows sampled nucleons and hotspots, with optional parent-connection lines. In this interactive view, circles denote protons and diamonds denote neutrons. Alpha colors identify the four clusters.

The second explorer shows isosurfaces of the summed 3D smooth density for both geometries. Its vertical axis is physical $z$. The surface levels and color scale are common to the two models. Hotspot density structure is resolved in the static slice plots above; hotspot centers are rotatable in the first explorer. The volume grid is for illustration, and is independent of the finer integration grids used in the audit.

14. How to use this notebook while developing¶

Change one control, then Run All. Use a different seed or event index to check that a feature is not specific to one example. Increase the geometry ensemble for the radial and pair statistics; increase the field ensemble for the mean and fluctuation maps. Increase spatial resolution when investigating narrow hotspot structure.

Use the appropriate invariant. Nuclear COM and per-parent hotspot weight are exact constraints. Radial distributions can change after hard-core rejection and recentering. Hotspot COM can fluctuate. Projected pairs can overlap. The smooth and hotspot fields coincide only after the appropriate ensemble average with the chosen convolution width.

Keep the layers separate. Nucleon sampling widths, hotspot offset widths, and source-profile widths describe different steps. A density slice uses fm$^{-3}$; thickness uses fm$^{-2}$ and integrates to $A$. The maps in this notebook provide geometry for the later GBW and finite-$A$ opacity calculation. They are not scattering amplitudes or coherent/incoherent cross sections.
